rows.en: Touya: "...Looks like the repairs still aren't finished.
Hey, Yamato, what should we... Yamato?
...Honestly, where the hell did she go?"
Touya: "What's this feeling...? Outside...?"
Touya: "This is... The crystal... It's making a sound...
This way...?"
Touya: "Oh... It stopped."
?????: "Lovely weather, isn't it?
You'd never believe it was raining until yesterday..."
Touya: "Wh-Who's there?!"
?????: "My apologies. I startled you."
Touya: "..."
?????: "Forgive my late introduction.
My name is Bernst Bulow."
Touya: "...What are you doing here?"
Bernst: "Can't you see?
I'm enjoying a spot of fishing..."
Touya: "I can see that.
I'm asking why you're fishing in a place like this.
It's pretty suspicious."
Bernst: "Even if you put it like that...
For someone who loves fishing, that's a foolish question.
Where there's water and the promise of fish, we cast a line...
That's the spirit of an angler.
Besides, this is a hidden gem known only to those in the know.
Why don't you join me?"
Touya: "You're a slippery one..."
Bernst: "Something that looked like a battleship landed
a little while ago. Are you a member of its crew?"
Touya: "..."
Bernst: "Oh, how rude of me to speak to you from here."
Bernst: "Now, coming to a place like this alone
suggests something's gone wrong aboard the ship,
and you're passing the time until it's fixed. Would that be right?"
Touya: "How do you know I was aboard that ship?"
Bernst: "Weren't you?"
Touya: "Well, yeah, I was, but..."
Bernst: "Come to think of it, I've heard of something called Spirit Mechs.
Do you know about them?"
Touya: "...That sounds awfully forced.
Who the hell are you?"
Bernst: "There's no need to be so wary.
I'm just an Alchemist who enjoys fishing.
More importantly, I'd like to ask why you pilot a Spirit Mech
and fight."
Touya: "What are you going to do with that answer?"
Bernst: "It's my own intellectual curiosity.
Why don't people stop fighting?
Well, I'm interested in the emotions people feel
in such situations."
Touya: "...You don't seem to be lying..."
Bernst: "Haven't you ever had doubts
about fighting yourself?"
Touya: "Of course I have!
Who the hell would choose to fight because they enjoy it?"
Bernst: "I see. You're afraid."
Touya: "Huh?"
Bernst: "Even if circumstances left you no choice,
you're afraid to fight.
That's what I'm saying."
Touya: "What?!"
Bernst: "Can you say that's wrong?
Can you say you're not afraid of fighting becoming normal, and one day
no longer feeling anything about killing people?"
Touya: "..."
Bernst: "Hmm, let's see...
Then why do you think it's wrong to kill people?"
Touya: "...Isn't it obvious...? Something like that..."
Bernst: "That's why I'm asking you for the reason."
Touya: "The reason...? Well...
because life is precious... That's why."
Bernst: "Then why is life precious?"
Touya: "Dead people... don't come back to life. That's why."
Bernst: "That's right. That's why people fear death.
When you die, everything becomes nothing.
But... That's only true for the person who dies, isn't it?"
Touya: "What?"
Bernst: "Even if someone else dies, as long as you're alive,
the world goes on. Because what perceives the world
is your own consciousness.
When you die, that consciousness vanishes, and at the same time,
the world vanishes, too."
Touya: "Don't be stupid! The world will still be here even if I die!
Of course it will!"
Bernst: "But you won't be able to perceive it.
So for you, it's the same
as the world having vanished."
Touya: "No, I mean, well, that might be how it is
inside my head, but... Aah! How do I put this?!"
Bernst: "Perhaps you could call it the difference between subjectivity and objectivity,
for example. But in the end, people
can never escape their subjective viewpoint completely."
Touya: "Wait, wait! I'm not following you!
What the hell are you trying to say?!"
Bernst: "People fear killing others
because they don't want to die themselves.
If they die, everything ends."
Touya: "...What? You're saying I don't want to kill people
because I don't want to die myself?!"
Bernst: "It's an extreme argument, but it's one aspect of the truth.
Not the whole of it, of course."
Touya: "...I can't just let that go.
Are you saying people are that selfish?"
Bernst: "Yes. People are bundles of ego.
For example, we spoke of life being precious, didn't we?
Does that idea apply to all life equally?
It doesn't, does it? That's logic limited strictly to 'human' life
and nothing else."
Touya: "That's not true. We don't take animals' lives
for no reason, either."
Bernst: "That's a projection of the ego.
Animals aren't the only things that are alive.
Plants and bacteria have lives, too.
But normally, you hardly ever think about the lives of plants or bacteria,
do you? Animals are relatively close to humans.
That makes it easier to project yourself onto them.
It's impossible to preach the dignity of life
for every living thing. That dignity is applied only to life-forms
that don't affect human interests."
Touya: "...So you mean people are nothing but hypocrites
in the end?"
Bernst: "I'm not condemning hypocrisy.
Even hypocrisy is a kind of good. Of course, it's good 'for humans,'
but I have no objection to hypocrisy.
Distinguishing our own species from all the rest
is an instinct every living thing possesses.
It's impossible to eliminate it.
But humans have the intelligence to restrain instinct.
You could also call it imagination.
That's what gives people objectivity.
The imagination to consider other people's pain makes us afraid
to hurt or kill them."
Touya: "You're contradicting yourself.
You just said people couldn't escape
their subjective viewpoint."
Bernst: "Yes. Ultimately, that's true.
I don't want to be killed, so I don't want to kill anyone.
But what about other people?
Do they think the same way I do?
Or do they think in ways
utterly different from mine?
Yes... That's when you realize that you yourself
are your entire world. Other people's worlds of consciousness
belong to other people, and no one else.
That fear led people to make rules.
'You must not hurt or kill others,' for example.
That's the limit of human objectivity.
If rules and laws mark the limit of objectivity, then the limit of subjectivity
is morality and religion. Both of these
set standards for human behavior.
After all, if you follow subjective thought to its conclusion,
everything other than yourself becomes 'nothing.'
So you need a safety valve to stop thinking somewhere.
What points you toward that stopping place is morality
and religion."
Touya: "...Are you trying to recruit me into a religion?"
Bernst: "Of course not. I'm only a meddlesome hypocrite who wants
to help you get back on your feet. In the end,
you're the only one who can solve your problems.
Communication through words has its limits.
I'm only laying out arguments that might
be useful to you.
I'd be glad if you could take
something away from them."
Touya: "...I can't believe everything you say
is right."
Bernst: "Of course. If I were right about everything,
I wouldn't have to struggle so much."
Touya: "So you're telling me to find my own standards
for how to act? To think about what justifies fighting
and possibly killing someone?"
Bernst: "It's enough if it works for you,
even if it doesn't hold together logically. You're looking for
too much meaning and logic in this.
Your subjective viewpoint doesn't need logic.
If you worry about justification, you'll go around in circles.
Ultimately, all logic breaks down."
Touya: "Hmph... You really are a hypocrite."
Bernst: "Heh heh heh... To me, that's a compliment."
Touya: "Still... Well, I do feel a bit better
somehow. Maybe it's just my imagination."
Bernst: "Do you? I'm glad..."
Yamato: "Touya!"
Bernst: "Oh, it seems your companion's looking for you.
I'll be on my way, then."
Touya: "Yeah."
Bernst: "One last thing. Could you tell me
your name?"
Touya: "Oh, yeah, I hadn't told you.
I'm Touya. Touya Kazami."
Bernst: "Well then, Touya, goodbye..."
Yamato: "Oh, there you are.
What are you doing out here?"
Touya: "Oh, just something. What's up?"
Yamato: "Oh, right.
It looks like the Liebhofen's fixed."
Touya: "I see. Thanks for coming all this way.
All right, let's head back."
Ymir: "Welcome back.
My, you look as though a weight's been lifted off your shoulders."
Touya: "Well, yeah. Anyway, Clovis and Arthur
aren't back yet?"
Ymir: "No. I wonder how far they've gone..."
Celica: "Shouldn't we call them back soon?"
Ymir: "You're right."
Clovis: "That terrorist's machine is heading your way.
We're pursuing it, but I don't think we can stop it."
Touya: "Why are you pursuing it?"
Arthur: "We didn't think there was any need to fight,
so we let it pass. We never expected it to know the Liebhofen's
position."
Touya: "Don't tell me..."
Miyasco: "I'm picking up an Armored Mech!
It's that terrorist's machine, all right."
Ymir: "...It seems they've spotted us..."
Touya: "Let's fight."
Celica: "You're eager."
Touya: "Running away won't solve anything.
I thought I'd try facing
what it means to fight head-on."
Fain: "That's the spirit! I like it!
All riiight! I'll..."
Celica: "Oh, not you, Fain. Mireon's still broken, isn't it?"
Fain: "Nooo..."
Ymir: "Then first, let's take the Liebhofen
up. Once optical cloaking is deployed,
we'll have the Spirit Mechs descend."
Touya: "Understood. I'm heading out, then."
